title: Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Learning Partial Differential Equations
authors_full: Zongyi Li*, Hongkai Zheng*, Nikola Kovachki, David Jin, Haoxuan Chen, Burigede Liu, Kamyar Azizzadenesheli, Anima Anandkumar

verification: full-text verified (all 27 pages read: main text pp.1-17, references pp.18-21, Appendices A-E pp.22-27)
subdomain: chaotic 2-d Kolmogorov flow (vorticity form, Re=500) with zero-shot super-resolution and Reynolds-number transfer; 2-d lid-driven cavity (no-slip walls, velocity-pressure form); 1-d Burgers; 2-d Darcy subsurface flow; inverse coefficient-function recovery
industry_context: No named deployment; carried out on NVIDIA NGC and Caltech Resnick HPC Center (Acknowledgements, p.17). Motivation: training data for operator learning can be 'expensive to generate, unavailable, or available only as low-resolution observations' (p.1); motivating applications cited include carbon capture and storage modeling (refs 54-55), weather/climate modeling (refs 19, 23), turbulence. Serves scientific machine learning / computational fluid dynamics surrogate modeling
problem_class: operator (learns the solution operator G-dagger: a -> u over a parametric PDE family; also solves single instances via instance-wise fine-tuning and inverse problems via forward and inverse operator models)
physics_enforced_exact: 1-d Burgers' equation (nu=0.01): d/dx1 u(x,t) + d/dx2(u(x,t)^2/2) = nu d/dx22 u(x,t), x in (0,1), t in (0,1]; u(x,0)=u0(x); periodic boundary conditions (Eq. 18). 2-d steady-state Darcy Flow, 'second order linear elliptic PDE with a Dirichlet boundary', a in L-infinity((0,1)^2; R+) piecewise constant, f=1: -div(a(x) grad u(x)) = f(x), x in (0,1)^2; u(x)=0 on the boundary (Eq. 19); both strong form L_pde(u) = div(a grad u) - f and weak/variational form L_pde(u) = -(1/2)<a grad u, grad u> - <u, f>, u in H^1 ('Experiments show the strong form has a better performance'). 2-d Navier-Stokes for a viscous incompressible fluid in vorticity form on the unit torus: d/dt w(x,t) + u(x,t).grad w(x,t) = nu Laplacian w(x,t) + f(x); div u = 0; w(x,0) = w0(x) (Eq. 20). Three settings: long temporal transient t in [0,50], l=1, Re=20; chaotic Kolmogorov flow t in [t0, t0+1], l=2pi, Re=500; lid cavity flow t in [5,10], l=1, Re=500 with no-slip u(x,t)=(0,0) at left/bottom/right walls and u(x,t)=(1,0) on top, solved in velocity-pressure formulation with the divergence-free condition in the residual
pde_type: multiple (Burgers: nonlinear viscous/parabolic; Darcy: linear elliptic, solved in strong and weak form; Navier-Stokes: viscous incompressible in vorticity form, chaotic regime)
dimensionality: 1-d Burgers (space+time, maps u0 to u(.,1)); 2-d steady Darcy; 2-d Navier-Stokes (2-d space + time, evaluated at up to 256x256x65); 2-d lid cavity 65x65x50
nonlinearity: mixed-to-strongly nonlinear: Burgers has quadratic flux u^2/2 and Navier-Stokes has advective nonlinearity u.grad w on the chaotic Kolmogorov attractor (Re=500); Darcy PDE is linear but the coefficient-to-solution operator G-dagger is not (paper: 'although the PDE is linear, the operator G-dagger is not')
bcs_ic_handled: Burgers: periodic BCs; IC u(x,0)=u0(x) is the operator input. Darcy: homogeneous Dirichlet u=0, 'enforced by multiplying a mollifier m(x) = sin(pi x) sin(pi y) for all methods' (Appendix A.2, hard output transform); forcing fixed f=1. Navier-Stokes/Kolmogorov: periodic BCs on the unit torus; initial vorticity w0 is the input. Lid cavity: no-slip walls imposed softly via loss terms - 'We minimize the residual error on the velocity, the divergence-free condition, as well as the initial condition and boundary condition. The weight parameters (alpha, beta) between different error terms are all chosen as 1' (Appendix B.2). Dynamic PDE loss carries an IC penalty beta*||u_theta|_{t=0} - a||^2 (Eq. 4). Non-periodic domains handled by Fourier continuation (zero-padding into a larger periodic space, Appendix C)
enforcement_mechanism: soft-penalty on an operator ansatz (PDE residual loss J_pde added to the operator data loss, with an anchor operator loss during instance-wise fine-tuning) + weak/variational form option for Darcy; derivatives of the operator output are computed exactly in function space via Fourier-space differentiation rather than per-point autodiff
enforcement_details: Physics enters as an equation loss evaluated on the neural operator's output function, combined with data: J_data = (1/N) sum_j int_D |u_j(x) - G_theta(a_j)(x)|^2 dx (Eq. 6), J_pde = E_{a~mu}[L_pde(a, G_theta(a))] (Eq. 7). 'One can sample an unlimited amount of virtual PDE instances by drawing additional initial conditions or coefficient conditions a_i ~ mu' (Section 3.1). Stationary loss (Eq. 3) = ||P(a,u_theta)||^2_{L^2(D)} + alpha||u_theta|_{dD} - g||^2; dynamic loss (Eq. 4) = ||du_theta/dt - R(u_theta)||^2 + alpha||u_theta|_{dD} - g||^2 + beta||u_theta|_{t=0} - a||^2. Three derivative methods (Section 3.3): (1) numerical differentiation (finite difference O(n), Fourier O(n log n)); (2) pointwise autograd via a query function u(x) = Q(v_L(x)) written as a truncated Fourier series (Eqs. 12-14); (3) function-wise differentiation - derivatives written exactly on Fourier space by chain rule, u' = Q'(v_L) * F^-1(i2pi k/D * (F v_L)) (Eq. 15), higher-order derivatives likewise, computable with the FFT on uniform grids. Fourier continuation: zero-padding embeds non-periodic problems in a periodic cube; loss computed in the original space (Appendix C). Instance-wise fine-tuning minimizes L_pde + alpha*L_op with anchor loss L_op(theta_i) = ||G_{theta_i}(a) - G_{theta_0}(a)||^2_{L^2_mu} against the frozen learned operator ('The anchor loss is a hard constraint that makes the optimization much easier', p.13). Inverse problems: forward model J_forward = L_pde(a_hat, u_dagger) + L_data(G_theta(a_hat)) + R(a_hat) (Eq. 16); inverse model J_backward = L_pde(F_theta(u_dagger), u_dagger) + L_op(F_theta(u_dagger), F_{theta_0}(u_dagger)) + R(F_theta(u_dagger)) (Eq. 17), R(a) = total variance for the piecewise-constant Darcy coefficient
network_architecture: Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) backbone: pointwise lifting P, L=4 Fourier layers v_{t+1} = sigma(W v_t + K_t v_t) with Fourier convolution operator (K v)(x) = F^-1(R . (F v))(x), R learnable on truncated modes, pointwise projection Q. Default width=64, mode=8 or 12, L=4 (Appendix A); Burgers width=64, mode=15; Darcy width=64, mode=20, depth=4; lid cavity width=32, mode=20 (velocity-pressure outputs). Kernel-integral first/last layers (graph kernel operators) can be mixed with Fourier layers for non-uniform meshes (Sections 2.4, 3). Built on the neural-operator framework of Li et al. [31] restricted to the Fourier convolution kernel [29]
activation_function: GeLU ('we use Fourier neural operator backbone with width = 64, mode = 8 or 12, L = 4, and GeLU activations', Appendix A)
input_representation: grid evaluations of the input function a on a uniform mesh: initial condition u0 for Burgers (u0 ~ N(0, 625(-Delta+25I)^-2)); initial vorticity w0 for NS (Gaussian random field, Li et al. [29]/[32] settings); diffusion coefficient field a for Darcy (a ~ psi#N(0,(-Delta+9I)^-2) thresholded to values 12 if a(x)>=0, 3 if a(x)<0); velocity-pressure fields for lid cavity; lifted by pointwise P to a higher co-dimension channel space
output_representation: solution function u evaluated on the grid: u(.,1) for Burgers; vorticity trajectory w up to T for NS; velocity in x,y and pressure fields for lid cavity; recovered coefficient a for the inverse model. Derivatives Dv_L and Du are computed in their exact forms at any query point (via Fourier-space function-wise differentiation) and fed to the equation loss; a query function allows evaluation on non-uniform meshes
loss_terms: Operator learning: L = J_data + J_pde (J_data Eq. 6, J_pde Eq. 7); stationary L_pde (Eq. 3) = interior PDE residual^2 + alpha * boundary mismatch^2; dynamic L_pde (Eq. 4) = ||du_theta/dt - R(u_theta)||^2 + alpha*BC + beta*IC terms, hyperparameters alpha, beta > 0. Darcy: strong form div(a grad u) - f or weak form -(1/2)<a grad u, grad u> - <u,f>. Instance-wise fine-tuning: L = L_pde + alpha*L_op (anchor loss vs frozen operator, Section 3.2). Inverse: J_forward = L_pde(a_hat, u_dagger) + L_data(G_theta(a_hat)) + R(a_hat); J_backward = L_pde(F_theta(u_dagger), u_dagger) + L_op(...) + R(F_theta(u_dagger)), R = total-variation regularization (Eq. 16-17)
loss_weighting: fixed weights: alpha = beta = 5 for long temporal transient flow (Appendix A.3); (alpha, beta) = 1 for lid cavity (Appendix B.2); PINN baselines grid-search boundary-loss weight from 10 to 100. No adaptive/NTK/self-adaptive weighting used (authors note such PINN techniques could be transferred to PINO)
sampling_strategy: uniform grids; PDE loss imposed at higher resolution than the data: Burgers data 32x25 (spatio-temporal) with J_pde at 128x100; Darcy data at spatial resolution 11x11 with J_pde at 61x61; Kolmogorov data 64x64x33 with J_pde at 256x256x65 (Table 1). Virtual PDE instances generated by sampling new ICs/coefficients from mu: 2200 PDE instances (Tables 1, 3), 160k (Table 4), 40k-400k (Table 7). No adaptive/residual-refinement collocation sampling
optimizer_schedule: Adam: lr 0.001 decaying by half every 100 epochs, 500 epochs total for Burgers (Appendix A.1); same hyperparameters for Darcy (A.2); lid cavity: Adam lr 0.0005 halved every 5000 iterations, 5000 iterations total (B.2); inverse-problem optimization converges with 200 iterations (Section 4.3); instance-wise fine-tuning uses gradient descent with optional progressive grid-resolution increase and last-layer fine-tuning (Section 3.2); PINN baselines use two-step optimization (Adam and L-BFGS) following NSFnet practice via DeepXDE/TensorFlow
training_compute: Nvidia V100 GPUs and A100 GPUs (Appendix A); Burgers training about 20 minutes on a single Nvidia 3090 GPU; Darcy around 1 hour on a single Nvidia V100 GPU; Kolmogorov T=0.125 operator model 'takes up to 2 days to train the model on a single Nvidia V100 GPU' (A.4); lid-cavity instance-wise fine-tuning 2 minutes; PINO offline training for Darcy inverse around 1 hour on a single GPU, vs considerably longer to deploy a finite element solver and an MCMC solver (p.17)
transfer_or_pretraining: Two-phase scheme: operator-learning phase (pretraining over multiple PDE instances) then instance-wise fine-tuning per instance. Explicit transfer across Reynolds numbers: 'we train the source operator model on one Reynolds number and then fine-tune the model to another Reynolds number, on the Kolmogorov flow with T = 1... PINO can be easily transferred to different Reynolds numbers ranging from 100 to 500' (p.14, Table 8, Figure 8). Transfer to different boundary conditions/geometries named as a future direction
uq_method: none for PINO itself; the Darcy inverse study uses accelerated MCMC (Cotter et al. [8], 500,000 steps) as a reference baseline reporting posterior mean with 4.52% error and 90.30% accuracy ('the Bayesian method outputs the posterior distribution, which is beyond obtaining a maximum a posteriori estimation', p.16). No Bayesian/ensemble UQ of the network
data_regime: physics-only possible (0 data samples) or any amount of low-resolution data combined with physics. Burgers: 1000 initial conditions, 800 low-resolution data instances (32x25) + 1000 PDE instances (Table 1). Darcy: 1000 coefficient conditions, 500 low-resolution instances (11x11). Kolmogorov: 800 low-res data (64x64x33) + 2200 PDE instances (Table 1); training sets of 400 or 4000 data points with up to 400k additional PDE instances (Table 7); chaotic T=0.5 set: 4000 ICs. Ground truth from numerical solvers (pseudo-spectral / finite difference); no experimental data
datasets_used: 1-d Burgers equation (nu=0.01, T=1, periodic); 2-d steady Darcy flow on unit box (piecewise-constant coefficient 12/3, f=1, Dirichlet); 2-d Navier-Stokes vorticity form on unit torus: long temporal transient (Re=20, T=50, l=1), chaotic Kolmogorov flow (Re=500, T=0.125/0.5/1, l=2pi), lid cavity flow (Re=500, T=[5,10], l=1, no-slip); all following the Li et al. [29]/[32] FNO-benchmark settings
baselines_compared: PINN (Raissi et al. [44]); LAAF-PINN (Jagtap et al. [21]) and SA-PINN (McClenny & Braga-Neto [39], cf. PINN-A07), implemented in DeepXDE with TensorFlow, two-step Adam+L-BFGS; PI-DeepONet (physics-informed DeepONet, Wang et al. [52]); DeepONet (Lu et al. [36]); data-driven FNO (Li et al. [29], cf. PINN-B13); 'ENO' column of Table 6 (per caption the data-only operator trained on 32x32x17); GPU-based pseudo-spectral solver (He & Sun [17]); conventional solver + accelerated MCMC (Cotter et al. [8]) for the Darcy inverse problem; UNet with trilinear interpolation for the super-resolution spectrum comparison (Figure 1)
evaluation_metrics: relative L2 error (solution error, averaged over 20-300 test instances with standard error); equation error (PDE residual norm, Table 7); wall-clock runtime (s); classification accuracy and relative L2 on the recovered coefficient a for the Darcy inverse problem; qualitative spectrum comparison for zero-shot super-resolution
key_quantitative_results: Physics constraints remove cross-resolution degradation (Table 1, data-only vs data+PDE, at 1x/2x/4x data resolution): Burgers 0.32/3.32/3.76% vs 0.17/0.28/0.38%; Darcy 5.41/9.01/9.46% vs 5.23/1.56/1.58%; Kolmogorov 8.28/8.27/8.30% vs 6.04/6.02/6.01%. Burgers physics-only (no data): PINO 0.38% vs PI-DeepONet 1.38%. Darcy (Table 2): DeepONet with data 6.97+-0.09%, PINO with data 1.22+-0.03%, PINO w/o data 1.50+-0.03%. Kolmogorov Re=500 T=0.125, eval 256x256x65 (Table 3): 0 data/2200 PDE instances 6.22+-0.11%; 800 data 6.01+-0.12%; 2200 data 5.04+-0.11%. Long temporal transient (Re=20, T=50, N=4800 data): PINO 2.87% vs FNO 3.04%; with test-time optimization (anchor + PDE loss) 1.84%; PINN and PINO-from-scratch fail (error > 50%). Instance-wise fine-tuning, chaotic Kolmogorov Re=500 T=0.5 (Table 4): PINN 18.7% at 4577s; PINO (0 data, fine-tuned) 0.9% at 608s; PINO (0.4k data + 160k PDE instances) 0.9% at 473s - 'PINO outperforms PINN and its improved variants by 20x smaller error and 25x speedup' (p.14). Zero-shot super-resolution: trained 64x64x32, evaluated 256x256x65; PINO spectrum overlaps ground truth beyond training frequencies. Inverse Darcy: inverse model 2.29% rel L2 on u and 97.10% classification accuracy on a; forward model 6.43%/95.38%; MCMC 4.52%/90.30%; PINO 3000x faster than MCMC (p.16). Lid cavity: 14.52% relative error in 2 minutes (65x65x50). Resolution convergence (Table 5, dx=2^-7, dt=2^-10): rel L2 0.0034, matching the differentiation method's convergence rate
errors_reported: Table 1 (1x/2x/4x data resolution): Burgers data 0.32+-0.01/3.32+-0.02/3.76+-0.02%, data+PDE 0.17+-0.01/0.28+-0.01/0.38+-0.01%; Darcy data 5.41+-0.12/9.01+-0.07/9.46+-0.07%, data+PDE 5.23+-0.12/1.56+-0.05/1.58+-0.06%; Kolmogorov data 8.28+-0.15/8.27+-0.15/8.30+-0.15%, data+PDE 6.04+-0.12/6.02+-0.12/6.01+-0.12%. Table 6 (trained on 32x32x17, T=0.125): ENO 9.73+-0.15/9.74+-0.16/9.84+-0.16% vs PINO 6.30+-0.11/6.28+-0.11/6.22+-0.11% at 64x64x33/128x128x33/256x256x65. Table 7 (Re=500, T=0.5, avg over 300 instances): 4k data + 400k PDE instances: 24.22/23.95/20.10% (128/64/32 resolutions; equation error down to 1.4596); 0 data + 100k PDE: 74.36-74.46% (physics-only fails on the longer chaotic horizon). Table 8 (Reynolds transfer, avg over 40): test Re=500: 0.0493 from scratch vs 0.0346 fine-tuned from Re=250 operator; test Re=100: 0.00234 from scratch vs 0.00237 (best transfer ~0.0022 at Re=200 source? no - 0.00223/0.00237 range). Lid cavity 14.52%. Burgers physics-only 0.38%. Long transient 2.87% -> 1.84% (FNO 3.04%)
speedup_claims: 'On average, the relative error is 7% lower on both transient and Kolmogorov flows, while matching the speedup of data-trained FNO architecture (400x) compared to the GPU based pseudo-spectral solver [17]' (p.2); long-temporal transient: 'PINO outputs the full trajectory in one step, which leads to a 400x speedup compared to the GPU solver' (Figure 9 caption); 'PINO outperforms PINN and its improved variants by 20x smaller error and 25x speedup' (p.14; Table 4 wall-clock 473s vs 4577s); Darcy inverse: 'PINO methods are 3000x faster compared to MCMC' (500,000 steps, p.16) and 'this approach is 3000x faster than the conventional solvers using accelerated Markov Chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC)' (p.3); learned-operator inference 'is extremely fast since it is performing inference on the neural operator' (p.8)
ablations: (1) data-only vs data+PDE loss across 1x/2x/4x data resolutions (Table 1): imposing J_pde at higher resolution restores accuracy on high-resolution test data (Darcy 9.01% -> 1.56% at 4x). (2) Data amount vs PDE instances (Tables 3, 7): more low-res data eases optimization (6.22% -> 6.01% -> 5.04%); additional PDE instances consistently improve generalization (4k data: 25.15% -> 24.15% (+100k) -> 24.22% (+400k) at 128x128x65, with equation error improving monotonically 1.8223 -> 1.6112 -> 1.4596). (3) Instance-wise fine-tuning vs pure operator inference (Table 4, Figure 4): 2.87% -> 0.9% on chaotic Kolmogorov; learned-operator ansatz converges faster than PINN-style pointwise optimization. (4) Resolution sweep under instance-wise optimization (Table 5): error decreases with finer dx/dt given longer gradient descent (0.0582 -> 0.0034); PINO inherits first-order-in-time (FD) and exponential-in-space (Fourier) convergence of its differentiation method. (5) Reynolds transfer (Table 8, Figure 8): fine-tuning from a source-Re operator beats from-scratch in accuracy and convergence speed for all Re in {100,...,500}. (6) Differentiation methods (Section 3.3): numerical (fast, noisy, resolution-limited), autograd (exact but slower and memory-heavy), function-wise Fourier (exact and efficient). (7) Additional baselines (Appendix B.1): LAAF-PINN and SA-PINN converge faster than vanilla PINN 'but there is still a big gap with PINO'; contributions 'orthogonal'. (8) Forward vs inverse operator model for Darcy inversion (Figure 7): inverse model best (2.29% vs 6.43% on u)
stated_limitations: Section 5 (p.17): 'since PINO is currently implemented with the FNO backbone with the Fast-Fourier transform, it is hard to extend to higher dimensional problems. Besides, when fine-tuning PINO using gradient descent methods does not converge as fast as using a finer grid as in Table 5. Further optimization techniques are yet to be developed.' Also: 'how to overcome the hard trade-off of accuracy and complexity' is an open direction. Section 3.2: instance-wise fine-tuning improves accuracy 'while incurring more computational costs', and higher resolution 'may potentially make the optimization unstable'. Appendix A.4 (p.23): 'The authors acknowledge that there could exist more sophisticated variants of PINN that perform better in our test cases.' Section 2.4: FNO aliasing error is inevitably present (deemed acceptable in practice)
failure_modes: PINN fails on multi-scale dynamic PDE systems due to optimization challenges: challenging optimization landscape, hyper-parameter sensitivity, spectral bias to high frequencies, and difficulty propagating IC/BC information to unseen interior/future times (Sections 1.2, 2.2). 'Neither the PINN nor PINO (from scratch) can handle this case (error > 50%), no matter solving the full interval at once or solving per smaller steps' on the long temporal transient flow (p.13). Plain neural operator in inverse problems is 'vulnerable under perturbation and shift of the input a' (domain shift, Figure 6b) - mitigated by the PDE constraint. Numerical differentiation errors 'will be amplified on the output solution'; autograd 'is usually slower and memory-consuming'. UNet+trilinear interpolation shows 'nosing [noisy] prediction with oscillating high frequencies' in super-resolution (p.14). Physics-only training collapses on the longer chaotic horizon (74% error at T=0.5 with 0 data, Table 7). GPU pseudo-spectral solver can be more effective than gradient-descent fine-tuning at high resolutions on chaotic Kolmogorov flow (Figure 9b)
reproducibility: No code or data URL is printed in the PDF (arXiv:2111.03794v4; journal DOI 10.1145/3648506). Full implementation details in Appendix A: FNO backbone (width 64, mode 8/12, L=4, GeLU), per-experiment hyperparameters and search grids; PINN baselines implemented with the DeepXDE library (TensorFlow backend) following the NSFnet two-step Adam+L-BFGS practice; hardware Nvidia V100/A100/3090; errors averaged over 5-300 test instances with standard errors. No random seeds stated
quotable_finding: The PDE loss function added to PINO vastly improves generalization and physical validity in operator learning compared to purely data-driven data methods. (p.2)
relevance_rqs: RQ2: component evidence - FNO backbone with soft PDE-residual loss, anchor operator loss for fine-tuning, and three derivative-computation mechanisms (numerical / autograd / exact function-wise Fourier). RQ3: physics+mechanism - PDE constraints imposed at higher resolution than the training data, unlimited virtual instances sampled from mu, weak/variational form for Darcy, Fourier continuation for non-periodic BCs. RQ1: problem classes - forward operator learning, instance-wise equation solving, and inverse coefficient recovery on fluids/transport benchmarks. RQ4: reliability evidence - zero-shot super-resolution, Reynolds-number transfer, convergence-with-resolution study, and explicit stated limitations (hard to extend to higher dimensions, optimization trade-offs)
manuscript_section: S4 methods (operator-learning enforcement branch: soft physics constraints on an operator ansatz, multi-resolution training, derivative computation); S5 fluids paragraph (Kolmogorov flow, lid cavity, Burgers, Darcy); T1-T2 (operator-learning vs PINN/DeepONet/FNO comparison rows); compute trade-off figures (Figures 4, 9) for the efficiency discussion

notes_caveats: Analyzed PDF is arXiv v4 (29 Jul 2023), not the typeset ACM/IMS JDS version. All benchmarks are synthetic math-benchmarks (1-d Burgers, 2-d Darcy, 2-d NS); no 3-d case, and the authors state the FNO+FFT backbone is 'hard to extend to higher dimensional problems'. The headline zero-data success (6.22%, Table 3) is for the short T=0.125 window; physics-only training collapses on the longer chaotic horizon T=0.5 (74.36-74.46% error, Table 7) and on long temporal transients without data - an honest boundary of the 'no data needed' claim. In Table 4 the '0 data samples' PINO rows mean no data during fine-tuning, but the operator ansatz was pretrained on 400 data points (Appendix A.4 comparison study, p.23). The '25x speedup' claim vs Table 4 wall-clock (4577s/473s ~ 9.7x) is not directly reconcilable from the printed numbers (error ratio is ~20x). The Table 6 baseline column labeled 'ENO' is, per its caption, the data-only operator (FNO) trained on 32x32x17. 'Relative error is 7% lower' (p.2) is a relative reduction, not percentage points. PINN comparisons rely on DeepXDE implementations with a fixed hyperparameter grid; authors concede stronger PINN variants may exist. Weak form (Darcy) is evaluated but the strong form is reported as better performing. No UQ, no seeds, no code link in the PDF
